description: 70% hydration is the classic sourdough starting point: open crumb, dough you can still handle. Work out the water, starter, and salt for any flour weight.

examples.result: Add 450 g flour, 300 g water, 100 g starter, and 10 g salt. Total dough 860 g.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 500 × 0.20 = 100 g.
The starter is half flour and half water, so it brings 50 g of flour and 50 g of water.
Total water is 70% of the flour: 500 × 0.70 = 350 g. Water to add is 350 - 50 = 300 g.
Flour to add is 500 - 50 = 450 g. Salt is 2%: 500 × 0.02 = 10 g.
examples.title: 500 g flour at 70% hydration

examples.result: Add 900 g flour, 600 g water, 200 g starter, and 20 g salt. Total dough 1720 g.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 1000 × 0.20 = 200 g.
The starter brings 100 g of flour and 100 g of water.
Total water is 70% of the flour: 1000 × 0.70 = 700 g. Water to add is 700 - 100 = 600 g.
Flour to add is 1000 - 100 = 900 g. Salt is 2%: 1000 × 0.02 = 20 g.
examples.title: 1000 g flour at 70% hydration

faqs.answer: Yes. Seventy percent is the most common starting point in sourdough recipes, and it gives a real open crumb while the dough is still shapeable. If you have made a loaf or two at 60 or 65%, 70% is the natural next step.
faqs.question: Is 70% hydration the standard for sourdough?

faqs.answer: Because the starter already brings water. For 500 g of flour, 70% hydration means 350 g of water in total, and 100 g of starter brings 50 g of that water. You add the remaining 300 g. If you added all 350 g on top of the starter, the true hydration would be about 73%.
faqs.question: Why is the water to add only 300 g and not 350 g?

faqs.answer: The dough will be softer and stickier than you are used to, and that is normal. Wet your hands before folding, and let the stretch and folds do the work: the dough firms up noticeably over the first hour. If it still spreads flat at shaping, your flour may need a lower hydration, or the dough may be over-fermented.
faqs.question: My 70% dough feels too sticky. What do I do?

faqs.answer: 860 g: 450 g flour to add, 300 g water to add, 100 g starter, and 10 g salt. That makes one good-sized boule, about 800 g once baked.
faqs.question: How much dough does 500 g of flour make at 70%?

faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the simplest way to check a recipe. If a recipe says 500 g flour and 350 g water with 100 g starter, the true hydration is not 70%. Count the starter and it is 400 g of water over 550 g of flour, about 73%. Recipes that ignore the starter run two to three points wetter than they claim.
faqs.question: Can I use this to check a recipe I found online?

felicityNote: Seventy percent is where my loaves started looking like the ones in the books. The dough feels alarming for the first half hour, and then it comes together like it always knew what it was doing.

parts.meaning: Total flour in the dough, always 100% in baker's percentages. The starter's flour is part of it.
Total water as a share of total flour. At 70%, every 100 g of flour holds 70 g of water.
Starter as a share of total flour. At 20%, 500 g of flour takes 100 g of starter.
A 100% hydration starter is half flour and half water, so half its weight is flour and half is water.
Salt as a share of total flour. At 2%, 500 g of flour takes 10 g of salt.

formula.text: Starter = flour × starter %. Flour to add = flour - starter ÷ 2. Water to add = flour × hydration % - starter ÷ 2. Salt = flour × salt %.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the flour and water
howToSteps.text: Put the bowl on the scale, zero it, and weigh in the flour to add, then the water to add, holding back about 25 g of the water for now. The calculator already subtracted the starter's flour and water.

howToSteps.name: Add the starter and salt
howToSteps.text: Add the ripe starter, then the salt. Mix until no dry flour is left, then add the held-back water only if the dough feels like it can take it.

howToSteps.name: Rest, then fold
howToSteps.text: Cover the bowl and rest for 30 minutes. Then give the dough three or four sets of stretch and folds in the first two hours, with wet hands. The dough will firm up with each set.

howToSteps.name: Bulk ferment and shape
howToSteps.text: Let the dough rise until it is about half as big again, domed, and jiggly, then shape it gently. At 70% the dough will spread a little at shaping; a tight shape and a floured basket keep it in form.

lede: At 70% hydration the dough is soft and open-crumbed, and this is the classic starting point for a country-style sourdough loaf. Flour here means the total flour in the dough, including the flour inside the starter, so the hydration you ask for is the hydration you get.

name: 70% Hydration
summary: 500 g flour at 70% hydration: add 450 g flour, 300 g water, 100 g starter, 10 g salt.
title: Sourdough Calculator: 70% Hydration
tutorial: Seventy percent is the hydration most sourdough recipes are written around, and for good reason. The dough is soft enough to open up into the irregular holes people picture when they think of sourdough, and firm enough that you can still shape it without a bench scraper and a prayer. If you only ever bake at one hydration, this is the one to learn.

The maths runs on baker's percentages, with flour always at 100%. For 500 g of total flour at 70% hydration, the dough holds 350 g of water in total. Your starter brings 50 g of that water, because 100 g of starter at 100% hydration is half flour and half water, so you add 300 g of water to the bowl. The starter also brings 50 g of flour, so you add 450 g of flour. Salt stays at 2%, which is 10 g.

Here is the detail that catches people out. Many recipes quote 70% hydration while ignoring the starter, and that dough is really wetter than 70%. Add 350 g of water on top of 100 g of starter and the dough holds 400 g of water against 550 g of flour, which is about 73%. This calculator counts the starter's flour and water, the way King Arthur Baking says it should be counted, so 70% here means 70%.

At 70% the dough will feel sticky when you first mix it, and then it will change. Stretch and folds build the gluten, and by the third set the dough holds together, smooths out, and starts to resist the stretch. Wet hands are the whole trick: water on your fingers stops the dough clinging, and a dry hand in a 70% dough is a losing battle.

Hold back some water on your first bake at 70%. Mix in all but the last 25 g, feel the dough after the rest, and add the rest only if it wants it. Bread flour at 12% protein or more will take the full 70% happily. All-purpose flour absorbs less, and a 70% dough made with it can turn slack, so if all-purpose is what you have, the held-back water is your safety valve.
